about.title: Box Plots, Standard Deviation and Outliers
about.length_note: About 40 minutes. There are four short parts: build a box plot, find outliers, measure spread with standard deviation, and compare two players. Each part ends with a check question. You can pause between parts, and that won't change the lesson.

Box Plot: Five-Number Summary, IQR & Outliers

say.text: Welcome to class 48. Today we turn a pile of numbers into one picture, then use it to compare two players fairly. It takes about 40 minutes, in four short parts.

show.text: Box Plots, Standard Deviation and Outliers

say.text: The four parts are: build a box plot, spot outliers, measure spread with standard deviation, and compare two players. Comparing center and spread across data sets is a standard high-school skill.

show.text:
1. Build a box plot
2. Spot outliers
3. Standard deviation
4. Compare two players

say.text: Part 1 starts the same way every time: put the numbers in order, smallest to largest. Here are Kai's points in nine games. These numbers are made up for practice.

show.text: Kai's points in nine games, sorted

say.text: Quartiles cut a sorted list into four equal parts. Q1 is the 25th percentile, Q2 is the median, and Q3 is the 75th percentile.

show.text: Quartiles: Q1, Q2 (median), Q3

ask.q: Which quartile is the same thing as the median?
ask.why: Q2 is the 50th percentile, the middle of the sorted list. That is the median.

say.text: Kai has nine games, so the median is the 5th number: 12. Four numbers sit below it and four above. With an odd count, leave the median out of both halves.

show.text: Nine games

ask.q: A sorted list has 9 numbers. Which one is the median?
ask.why: The 5th number has 4 numbers on each side, so it is exactly in the middle.

say.text: Q1 is the median of the lower half: 6, 8, 9, 10. The middle two are 8 and 9, so Q1 is 8.5. Q3 is the median of the upper half: 13, 14, 15, 30, so Q3 is 14.5. A calculator may use a slightly different rule, so check what your class uses.

show.text:
Lower half: 6, 8, 9, 10 gives Q1 = 8.5
Median = 12
Upper half: 13, 14, 15, 30 gives Q3 = 14.5

ask.q: A lower half is 2, 4, 6, 10. What is Q1?
ask.why: With four numbers, the middle two are 4 and 6. Their average is 5.

say.text: Now we have five numbers: the smallest, Q1, the median, Q3, and the largest. Together they are called the five-number summary.

show.text: Kai's five-number summary

ask.q: Which of these is NOT part of the five-number summary?
ask.why: The five numbers are the smallest, Q1, the median, Q3 and the largest. The mean is not one of them.

say.text: Time to draw. Make a number line. Draw a box from Q1 to Q3, with a line inside at the median. For now, draw whiskers out to the smallest and largest values. We'll improve the whiskers soon.

show.text: A number line from 0 to 32. A box runs from 8.5 to 14.5 with a line inside at 12. A thin whisker reaches left to 6 and right to 30.

ask.q: Where is the median drawn on a box plot?
ask.right: As a line inside the box
wrong: At the left end of the left whisker
At the right edge of the box
At the far right of the plot
ask.why: The box runs from Q1 to Q3, and the median is the line inside it.

say.text: The width of the box has a name. The interquartile range, or IQR, is Q3 minus Q1. It is the range of the middle 50 percent of the data. For Kai, 14.5 minus 8.5 is 6.

ask.q: Q1 is 8.5 and Q3 is 14.5. What is the IQR?
ask.why: IQR is Q3 minus Q1, so 14.5 − 8.5 = 6. The number 24 is the largest minus the smallest, which is the range, not the IQR.

say.text: Part 2: outliers. An outlier is a value that sits far from the rest of the data. Kai's 30 looks far away, but 'looks far' is not a rule. So we use one.

show.text: Outlier: a value far from the rest

say.text: The rule uses the IQR. Multiply the IQR by 1.5. Subtract that from Q1 to get the lower fence. Add it to Q3 to get the upper fence. Values outside the fences are outliers.
Check Kai's games against the fences. The 30 is above 23.5, so it is an outlier. Every other game is between −0.5 and 23.5, so none of them is.

show.text: Outlier: 30 (above 23.5) | Not outliers: 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15

ask.q: Kai's smallest score is 6 and the lower fence is −0.5. Is 6 an outlier?
wrong: Yes, because it is the smallest score
Yes, because it is below Q1
No, because it is the median
ask.why: Only values below the lower fence or above the upper fence are outliers. Being the smallest is not enough.

say.text: Now we can fix the whiskers. Each whisker goes to the most extreme value that is not an outlier. The outlier gets its own dot. Kai's right whisker ends at 15, and the 30 is a dot.

show.text: The same number line. The box runs from 8.5 to 14.5 with a median line at 12. The left whisker reaches to 6 and the right whisker only to 15. A separate dot sits at 30.

ask.q: Where does Kai's right whisker end?
ask.why: The whisker stops at the largest value that is not an outlier, and that is 15. The fence at 23.5 is only a cutoff, not a real game score.

say.text: Why does it matter? One big game pulls the mean up. With the 30, Kai's mean is 13. Without it, the mean is about 10.9. The median only moves from 12 to 11.

show.text: Mean 13 with the 30, about 10.9 without

say.text: So should we delete outliers? Not automatically. An outlier can be a typo, a mistake, or real data. It should only be left out for a good reason.

show.text: Outliers can be typos, lies, or real data.

ask.q: Kai's 30 was a real game that he really scored. What should we do with it?
ask.right: Keep it, and say it was an unusually big game
wrong: Delete it, because outliers are always wrong
Delete it, because it makes the mean bigger
Change it to 15 so the plot looks neat
ask.why: The 30 is real data, so there is no good reason to remove it. We keep it and note that it is unusual.

say.text: Part 3: standard deviation. It is a number that tells the typical distance of the data from the mean. A small value means the numbers bunch close to the mean. A big value means they are spread out.

show.text: Standard deviation: the typical distance from the mean

say.text: Let's see it. Mia scored 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18, so her mean is 14. The distance of each score from 14 is 4, 2, 0, 2 and 4. Distance ignores direction, so it is never negative.

show.text: How far each of Mia's scores is from her mean of 14

ask.q: Mia's mean is 14. How far is her score of 18 from the mean?

say.text: The average of those distances is 2.4. The standard deviation is about 3.2. They are not identical, but they are close. Standard deviation is roughly the typical distance from the mean.

show.text: Mia: average distance 2.4, standard deviation about 3.2

say.text: Now Jo. Jo scored 4, 9, 14, 19 and 24. The mean is also 14, but the distances are 10, 5, 0, 5 and 10. Jo's standard deviation is about 7.9. Same mean, very different spread.

show.text: Mia: scores 10 to 18, standard deviation about 3.2 | Jo: scores 4 to 24, standard deviation about 7.9

ask.q: Mia's standard deviation is 3.2 and Jo's is 7.9. Whose scores stay closer to the mean?
ask.why: A smaller standard deviation means the data sit closer to the mean. Mia's is smaller.

say.text: You don't need to work this out by hand. A calculator or spreadsheet does it. You may see two versions, sx and σx. In this class we use the sample version, sx. Standard deviation is always zero or more.

show.text: Standard deviation is never negative

ask.q: Can a standard deviation be negative?
ask.right: No, it is always zero or more
wrong: Yes, if the data are below the mean
Yes, if the mean is negative
ask.why: Standard deviation measures distance, and distance is never negative. It is zero only when every value is the same.

say.text: One more fact about standard deviation. It reacts to outliers. Kai's standard deviation is about 7.0 with the 30, and about 3.1 without it. The IQR only goes from 6 to 5.

show.text:
With the 30: standard deviation about 7.0, IQR 6
Without the 30: standard deviation about 3.1, IQR 5

ask.q: When Kai's 30 is removed, which spread number changes MORE?
wrong: They change by the same amount
ask.why: One extreme game moves the standard deviation a lot, but it barely moves the IQR.

say.text: So choose the spread number to match the data. For fairly even, symmetric data, the mean and standard deviation work well. For lopsided data or data with outliers, the median and IQR are usually the safer pair.

show.text: Even, symmetric data: mean and standard deviation | Lopsided data or outliers: median and IQR

say.text: Part 4: compare two players. Put both box plots on one number line. Mia's box runs from 11 to 17. Jo's runs from 6.5 to 21.5. Both medians are 14.

show.text: One number line from 0 to 26 with two box plots stacked. Mia's box runs from 11 to 17 with a line at 14, and whiskers from 10 to 18. Jo's box runs from 6.5 to 21.5 with a line at 14, and whiskers from 4 to 24.

ask.q: Jo's box is much wider than Mia's. What does that tell us?
ask.right: Jo's middle 50% of games is more spread out
wrong: Jo scores more points than Mia
ask.why: The width of the box is the IQR. A wider box means the middle half of the data is more spread out. Their medians are the same.

say.text: Here are the numbers behind the picture. Mia's IQR is 6 and Jo's is 15. Mia's standard deviation is about 3.2 and Jo's is about 7.9. Both spread measures tell the same story.

show.text: Spread of Mia and Jo: standard deviation and IQR

say.text: When you compare two data sets, use four steps. Compare the centers. Compare the spreads. Look for outliers or lopsided shapes. Then say what it means in plain words about the game.

show.text:
1. Compare the centers
2. Compare the spreads
3. Check outliers and shape
4. Say it in words

ask.q: A coach wants a player who scores close to 14 almost every game. Mia and Jo both have a median of 14. Who should the coach pick?
ask.right: Mia, because her spread is smaller
wrong: Jo, because her spread is bigger
Either one, because the medians are equal
Jo, because her highest score is 24
ask.why: The centers are equal, so the spread decides. Mia's scores stay close to 14, so she is steadier.

say.text: One last check on your own. Team Red and Team Blue both have a median of 70 points. Red's standard deviation is 4 and Blue's is 12.

show.text: Team Red: median 70, standard deviation 4 | Team Blue: median 70, standard deviation 12

ask.q: Which team's scores are harder to predict from game to game?
wrong: You can't tell without the mean
ask.why: Blue's standard deviation is bigger, so its scores are more spread out and less predictable.

say.text: Well done. Today you built a box plot from a five-number summary and found outliers with the 1.5 times IQR rule. You also read standard deviation as typical spread and compared two players. Next class: two-way tables.

other_side.claim: A box plot's whiskers stop at the last non-outlier, and outliers show as dots.
other_side.other_view: Not every box plot works this way. A basic box-and-whisker plot always extends its whiskers to the minimum and maximum, with no outlier dots. The version with the 1.5 × IQR rule is sometimes called a modified box plot. Check which version your book or teacher uses.

other_side.claim: Outliers should be kept unless there is a good reason to remove them.
other_side.other_view: Some people remove outliers when they are clearly mistakes, such as a typo. Others keep every real value. The shared advice is to decide on purpose and explain the choice, not delete a point just because it is inconvenient.

other_side.claim: Standard deviation is the best way to describe spread.
other_side.other_view: It depends on the shape of the data. The standard says to use statistics appropriate to the shape of the data. Standard deviation suits symmetric data. With outliers or lopsided data, the IQR is often the better choice, because one extreme value moves the standard deviation a lot.
